notes.headline: Nvidia: revenue doubled to $115.8 billion, yet the shares fell — the guide implies a lower gross margin
notes.takeaway: Revenue rose 103% to $115.8 billion and adjusted EPS of $2.68 beat the $2.47 consensus by 8%. The outlook calls for about $130 billion next quarter, but with gross margin falling to 71–72% from 74.9% as the new Vera Rubin platform ramps. The shares fell 3.3%.
results: Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the quarter ended October 25, up 20% from the previous quarter and 103% from a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.68 against a consensus of about $2.47 and $1.27 a year ago; reported EPS was $2.70. Data Center revenue was $107.6 billion, up 110%, which is 93% of the company’s sales.

Gross margin was 74.9% on the adjusted basis, essentially flat on the prior quarter and 1.4 points higher than a year ago. Adjusted operating income was $77.9 billion, up 116%, on operating expenses of $8.8 billion — expenses grew 52% while revenue grew 103%, which is the operating leverage in one line.

The balance sheet grew with the business. Accounts receivable stood at $81.0 billion against $38.5 billion at the start of the fiscal year, and inventories at $39.7 billion against $21.4 billion. The company returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter through buybacks and dividends, and the board added $150 billion to the repurchase authorisation in September.
mgmt: The release quotes Colette Kress, named as interim chief executive as well as chief financial officer, saying the company’s momentum is real, that Vera Rubin is ‘off to an explosive start’ and that the product roadmap is on track. Nvidia describes the Vera Rubin NVL72 rack as the fastest product ramp in its history, with systems running at cloud partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and Oracle.

For the fourth quarter, which includes an extra week, Nvidia expects revenue of $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, and gross margin of 71.0% to 72.0%. Operating expenses are expected to be about $10.7 billion on the adjusted basis. The company said it is not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in that outlook.

Beyond the numbers the release is a list of the platform’s spread: Vera CPUs — Nvidia’s first fully custom data-centre processor — being adopted by cloud providers and AI developers, and expanded capacity for large model developers through cloud partners.
view: A company doubling revenue at this scale and beating estimates by 8% saw its shares fall, and the reason is in one line of the outlook: gross margin of 71% to 72%, down roughly three points from 74.9%. New platforms always ramp at lower margins — early yields are poorer and the product arrives as complete racks with more bought-in content — and Nvidia has been through this cycle with each generation. But three points on $130 billion of revenue is close to $4 billion of quarterly gross profit, and the market wants to know whether this is a ramp cost that reverses or the new level for a business selling whole systems rather than chips.

The revenue guide deserves a careful read too. $130 billion is 12% sequential growth, and the quarter has fourteen weeks instead of thirteen. Adjust for the extra week and underlying sequential growth is closer to 4% to 5%, after 20% this quarter. That is not weakness — the company is supply-constrained on a brand-new platform — but it is a visible deceleration, and a stock valued on acceleration notices it.

The working capital is the item I would study hardest. Receivables have more than doubled in nine months to $81 billion and inventory has nearly doubled to $40 billion. Both are what a product transition at this pace looks like, and both mean reported profit is running ahead of cash collected. Receivables of that size are concentrated in a handful of customers, some of them funding their purchases with debt and with capital from Nvidia’s own investments — the $44 billion of marketable equity securities on the balance sheet, up from $13 billion, shows how much Nvidia now holds in companies that buy from it. That circularity does not break while demand grows; it amplifies the downside if it stops.

None of this changes what Nvidia is: the supplier with no close substitute for the largest capital spending cycle in technology history, earning a 67% operating margin and now selling the processor, the networking and the rack. The China line — no data-centre compute revenue assumed — means any reopening is upside not in the numbers. The risk has never been the next quarter. It is that roughly 93% of revenue comes from one kind of customer making one kind of bet, and that the spending is set by a few boards of directors. The leadership situation, with the finance chief quoted as interim chief executive, adds an uncertainty the company has not faced in its history.
notes.watch: Gross margin in the January quarter against the 71–72% guide, and receivables relative to revenue. Margin recovering as Vera Rubin matures confirms a ramp cost; receivables growing faster than sales would say customers are taking longer to pay.
